zh.principle:
**攻击**：拖crib法（Crib Dragging）。### 密钥流重用的代数事实

设两条消息 P1、P2 使用同一条密钥流 K：

C1 = P1 ⊕ K，C2 = P2 ⊕ K。C1 ⊕ C2 = (P1 ⊕ K) ⊕ (P2 ⊕ K) = P1 ⊕ P2。密钥流 K 被完全消去，攻击者得到两条明文的异或。它仍然不是明文，但已经把“两条独立的加密消息”变成一个密切相关的问题。### 拖 crib 的基本操作

若攻击者猜 P1 在偏移 i 处含有已知词 w（长度为 ℓ），就把 w 与 (C1⊕C2)[i…i+ℓ-1] 异或，得到 P2 在对应位置的候选片段：

P2[i…i+ℓ-1] = (C1⊕C2)[i…i+ℓ-1] ⊕ w。如果候选片段可读，说明 w 很可能在 P1 中，同时 P2 的这一段也被恢复。把 w 滑过所有偏移，收集可读候选；再用语言模型、词表和更多密文交叉验证。### 从手工猜测到语言模型

手工拖 crib 依赖攻击者对明文的猜测。自动化方法把候选文本按语言模型打分：对候选字符序列计算 Σ log Pr(c_j | 上下文)，保留高分路径；再用动态规划或束搜索扩展。Mason 等的论文正是把这一过程系统化，报告在真实数据上可达到很高的字符准确率。
zh.why:
一次性密码本的安全性依赖密钥只使用一次。两条消息共用 K 后，K 不再是未知量，而是被异或消去的公共项。攻击者不需要恢复 K，只需要利用两条明文的语言结构。### 为什么 crib 不必很长

一段常见问候、HTML 标签、协议头或固定字段就足以作为锚点。候选片段可读性把“猜测是否正确”变成可检验的信号；一旦锚定，明文的两侧可以用语言模型继续扩展。### 对协议设计的含义

nonce/IV 的唯一性是流密码的生命线。SIV、GCM 的 nonce 管理、随机数生成和密钥轮换都必须保证同一密钥下不重复使用同一 nonce；否则 confidentiality 和 authenticity 可能一起失效。
zh.used:
1.确认两条或多条密文使用同一密钥流：检查 nonce、IV、计数器或协议实现。2.计算任意两条密文的异或，得到 P1⊕P2。3.选择可能的 crib：语言词、HTML 标签、协议头、已知文件名或固定错误消息。4.把 crib 滑过所有偏移，收集另一侧可读的候选；用词表、n-gram 或语言模型排序。5.用恢复的片段扩展相邻明文，并用第三条密文交叉验证；最后用重新加密验证假设。6.报告只能写“在假设同一密钥流下恢复的候选明文”，不能把候选当成已验证的原文。### 典型场景

一次性密码本的 nonce 重用、WEP 的 IV 重用、流密码实现错误、CTF 中的 many-time pad、以及任何把计数器/随机数误用为固定值的协议。
zh.broken: 1.密钥流从未重用：每条消息使用独立随机密钥或唯一 nonce，异或不出 P1⊕P2。2.使用认证加密且 nonce 管理正确：密文被篡改会被拒绝，重用也会被协议检测。3.明文语言未知或高度随机：crib 无法锚定，语言模型评分失效。4.消息太短或 crib 不在任何消息中：滑动窗口没有可读候选。5.明文经过压缩/加密/编码：候选片段不呈现自然语言结构。6.只恢复片段不等于恢复全文：需要更多密文、语言模型和外部约束。拖 crib 法是已知明文/猜测明文攻击，不是万能解密器；它利用的是密钥流重用，而不是算法本身的代数弱点。报告必须说明重用证据、crib 来源和候选验证方法。
zh.history:
密钥流重用的危险在一次性密码本的理论中早已明确：同一密钥加密两条消息，异或就消去密钥。传统密码分析依赖分析者猜测常见词或协议字段，再手工滑动比对。2006 年，Mason、Watkins、Eisner 与 Stubblefield 在 CCS 上发表自动化方法：把两条密文的异或当作约束，用统计语言模型和动态规划恢复最可能的明文对，并在真实数据上报告高准确率。这把“拖 crib”从手工技巧推进为可重复的语言模型攻击。### 今天的教训

WEP 的 IV 重用、流密码 nonce 管理错误和 CTF 的 many-time pad 反复说明：密钥流唯一性不是实现细节，而是安全定义的一部分。

en.principle:
**Attack**: Crib Dragging (拖crib法). ### The algebraic fact of keystream reuse

Let two messages P1 and P2 use the same keystream K:

C1 = P1 ⊕ K, C2 = P2 ⊕ K. XOR the two ciphertexts:

C1 ⊕ C2 = (P1 ⊕ K) ⊕ (P2 ⊕ K) = P1 ⊕ P2. The keystream K cancels completely, leaving the XOR of the two plaintexts. It is still not plaintext, but it turns “two independently encrypted messages” into one tightly coupled problem. ### The basic crib-dragging operation

If the attacker guesses that P1 contains a known word w of length ℓ at offset i, XOR w with (C1⊕C2)[i…i+ℓ-1] to obtain the candidate fragment of P2 at the corresponding position:

P2[i…i+ℓ-1] = (C1⊕C2)[i…i+ℓ-1] ⊕ w. If the candidate is readable, w is likely present in P1 and the corresponding segment of P2 has also been recovered. Slide w across every offset, collect readable candidates, and cross-check them with a language model, a word list and more ciphertexts. ### From manual guessing to a language model

Manual crib dragging depends on the attacker’s guess about the plaintext. An automated method scores candidate text with a language model: for a candidate character sequence it computes Σ log Pr(c_j | context), keeps high-scoring paths, and extends them with dynamic programming or beam search. Mason et al. systematised this process and reported high character accuracy on realistic data.
en.why:
The one-time pad relies on the key being used once. Once two messages share K, K is no longer an unknown; it is a common term cancelled by XOR. The attacker does not need to recover K, only to exploit the language structure of the two plaintexts.

A greeting, an HTML tag, a protocol header or a fixed field is enough as an anchor. Readability of the candidate turns “is the guess right?” into a testable signal; after anchoring, a language model can extend the plaintext on both sides.

Nonce/IV uniqueness is the lifeline of a stream cipher. SIV, GCM nonce management, random-number generation and key rotation must ensure that the same key never uses the same nonce twice; otherwise confidentiality and authenticity can fail together.
en.used:
1. Confirm that two or more ciphertexts use the same keystream: inspect the nonce, IV, counter or protocol implementation. 2. XOR any two ciphertexts to obtain P1⊕P2. 3. Choose plausible cribs: language words, HTML tags, protocol headers, known file names or fixed error messages. 4. Slide the crib across all offsets, collect readable candidates on the other side, and rank them with a word list, n-grams or a language model. 5. Extend the recovered fragments into adjacent plaintext and cross-check with a third ciphertext; finally re-encrypt to test the hypothesis. 6. The report may state “candidate plaintext under the same-keystream hypothesis”, not “verified original text”.

One-time-pad nonce reuse, WEP IV reuse, stream-cipher implementation errors, many-time pads in CTFs, and any protocol that mistakenly uses a fixed value as a counter or randomiser.
en.broken:
1. The keystream is never reused: each message uses an independent random key or a unique nonce, so XOR does not yield P1⊕P2. 2. Authenticated encryption with correct nonce management: tampering is rejected and reuse can be detected by the protocol. 3. The plaintext language is unknown or highly random: no crib anchors, and language-model scoring fails. 4. The messages are too short or the crib is in neither message: the sliding window produces no readable candidate. 5. The plaintext is compressed, encrypted or encoded: candidates do not show natural-language structure. 6. Recovering a fragment is not recovering the full text: more ciphertexts, language models and external constraints are needed.

Crib dragging is a known-plaintext or guessed-plaintext attack, not a universal decryptor; it exploits keystream reuse, not an algebraic weakness of the cipher. A report must state the reuse evidence, crib source and candidate verification.
en.history:
The danger of keystream reuse was clear in the theory of the one-time pad: encrypt two messages under one key and XOR cancels the key. Traditional cryptanalysis relied on the analyst guessing common words or protocol fields and sliding them by hand.

In 2006 Mason, Watkins, Eisner and Stubblefield published an automated method at CCS: treating the XOR of two ciphertexts as a constraint, they used a statistical language model and dynamic programming to recover the most probable plaintext pair, reporting high accuracy on realistic data. This moved crib dragging from a manual trick to a repeatable language-model attack.

WEP IV reuse, stream-cipher nonce mismanagement and many-time pads in CTFs repeatedly show that keystream uniqueness is part of the security definition, not an implementation detail.
